newsitem.title: Georgia: Separatist leader holds talks in Georgian capital.
newsitem.headline: Separatist leader holds talks in Georgian capital.

text.p: Vladislav Ardzinba, leader of Georgia's breakaway Abkhazia region, held unprecedented face-to-face peace talks with Georgian President Eduard Shevardnadze in the Georgian capital on Thursday.
Shevardnadze, making brief comments to reporters alongside Ardzinba, said he and the separatist leader would "probably sign a statement, an agreed one" after more talks.
Neither he nor Ardzinba shed any light on the statement and gave few details after several hours of talks.
Ardzinba was accompanied by Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov amid heavy security throughout the city. Primakov's visit had been announced but Ardzinba's presence was a surprise.
Shevardnadze and Ardzinba, bitter enemies since the 1992-93 conflict between Georgians and Abkhaz in which about 10,000 people were killed, briefly hugged before starting talks.
Ardzinba's visit is the first to Georgia since the war took place and five years to the day since Georgian troops entered the province to try to halt its moves towards independence.
"I think this visit is a big event on a very difficult day for our peoples. We've had an honest and sincere conversation," Shevardnadze said.
Ardzinba said: "We have come here to put an end to the confrontation, to find ways of mutual understanding. From that point of view the discussions that have taken place sow a certain optimism."
Talks between Georgia and Abkhazia on reaching a full political agreement have been deadlocked and the latest round of U.N.-mediated negotiations has produced no tangible results.
The subtropical Black Sea region has run itself as a de facto independent state since the war.
No state has recognised Abkhazia and Western diplomats and U.N. officials have told separatist leaders that there is no prospect that any will.

Abkhazia is one of several bloody conflicts which have bedevilled Georgia since independence from the Soviet Union in 1991. Shevardnadze, humiliated by the loss of what many consider the most beautiful and richest part of the country, sees his role in Georgian history as recovering the province.
Primakov has said he hopes to prepare a deal between Georgia and Abkhazia to pave the way for a formal peace agreement to be signed in Moscow in the presence of President Boris Yeltsin.

Yeltsin has recently supported the Georgian position that Abkhazia should be part of Georgia but receive wide autonomy, and that the separatist government should allow at least 150,000 ethnic Georgian refugees to return to their homes.
Abkhazia wants a type of "union state" confederation. This idea has been repeatedly rejected by Tbilisi.
Russia also has 1,500 peacekeepers in a buffer zone between Abkhazia and Georgia.

The mandate for the Russian troops expired on July 31 but they will stay in the zone until their fate can be decided by the leaders of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), which groups 12 former Soviet republics, in September.
A possible withdrawal of the contingent has stirred concern among political analysts, who say it could spark new bloodshed.

Georgia wants the peacekeepers to police more of Abkhazia and help resettle refugees. Commonwealth leaders approved the changes earlier this year but Russia has refused to take them up, citing Abkhaz objections.
Shevardnadze has urged Moscow not to ease sanctions against Abkhazia imposed two years ago by the CIS leaders.

A partial sea blockade, enforced almost entirely by Russian naval vessels, and strict restrictions on movement through the region's only land border -- with Russia -- have crippled Abkhazia's once thriving tourist-driven economy.
